source.title: Exploring Quaternion Neural Network Loss Surfaces

record.file_problem: none; the complete paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own loss-surface and training results, but does not test any listed claim version about benchmark classification error, local minima, depth, initialization, learning-rate stability, or batch normalization.
record.gate_note: The paper's claims about smoother quaternion loss surfaces and its breast-cancer classification results do not measure the training-error behavior named in the versions. Its Lorenz time-series training-loss results are recorded under fits_no_version because they concern regression, not classification.
record.test_reason: The study compares tuned quaternion and real-valued two-hidden-layer MLPs on Lorenz regression and breast-cancer classification. Its training-loss and projected-curvature results do not test any supplied version. Batch normalization, initialization and depth effects are discussed through prior work rather than tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors interpret both experiments as evidence of smoother quaternion loss surfaces and introduce a curvature estimator requiring no second-order derivatives. Their comparisons concern tuned final models; classification significance uses alpha=0.1, and they acknowledge that the large regression performance difference may bias the surface comparison toward the quaternion model.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains tuned, two-hidden-layer QNN and real-valued MLP models using SGD for regression and binary classification; it does not test the listed benchmark classification recipes or compare initializations, network depth, or normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: The tuned quaternion Lorenz predictor reportedly reaches near-zero training MSE after one epoch; the real-valued predictor retains training loss well above zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested Lorenz regression task, the tuned quaternion MLP reaches near-zero training loss substantially earlier than the tuned real-valued MLP.

fits_no_version.finding: Projected mean curvature is lower for quaternion models: classification 1.382e-5 versus 1.946e-5 (p=0.0874); regression 0.000112 versus 0.0503 (p<1e-43). These are comparisons around tuned final models, not training-dynamics tests.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested tuned quaternion MLPs have lower estimated projected loss-surface curvature than the real-valued comparators, with classification significance assessed at alpha=0.1.

record.code_released: not stated; data and code are available upon request.
record.problems: The study is limited to fully tuned models with two hidden layers and does not track loss surfaces throughout training; the authors note that the regression loss and surface plots may be biased in favor of the QNN because of its large performance advantage. The reported training-loss comparisons are for a regression task, not the classification benchmarks in the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The breast-cancer classification results report test accuracy and AUROC, not the training classification error named in the versions.

untested.parts: Convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels and effects of size, early stopping and regularization.
Spurious-minimum frequency in ReLU teacher-student problems and effects of extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, and the specified initialization and normalization exceptions.
Controlled initialization comparisons measuring training speed, signal propagation or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, transient loss increases, evolving sharpness and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The numeric regression errors in Table 5 are test-set metrics and must not be substituted for the qualitative training-loss values in R1–R2. Neither low projected curvature nor successful regression training establishes any supplied version.

versions.untested_parts: Benchmark classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels; model size, early stopping, and regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual networks, depth effects, and normalization.
Initialization effects on training speed or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability limits, curvature changes during training, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup training without normalization.

rows.subject: QNN predictor
rows.operation_detail: Trained for the Lorenz time-series prediction task; the text reports training loss after the first epoch.
rows.value: near-zero Mean Square Error loss on the 1000 step prediction task after the first training epoch
rows.note: Regression task; this result does not measure classification error. The paper gives no numeric training-loss value in the text.
rows.check: The reported near-zero MSE after one epoch is supported by Section 4.2, but measures regression loss rather than V1's convolutional-network training classification error. Table 4 specifies 32 neurons per hidden layer, not 32 total.

rows.subject: NN predictor
rows.operation_detail: Trained for the Lorenz time-series prediction task; the text reports training loss throughout training.
rows.value: remained well above zero throughout the entire training process while overfitting slightly to the training data
rows.note: Regression task; this result does not measure classification error. The paper gives no numeric training-loss value in the text.
rows.check: Section 4.2 explicitly reports training loss remaining above zero, but this regression result bears on no supplied version. Table 4 specifies 148 neurons per hidden layer, not 148 total.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
